lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: exponential decay and halving; Geology: dating rocks
lessons.smsc: Moral: responsibility for long-lived waste affecting future generations

keywords.def: the number of nuclei that decay each second, measured in becquerels (Bq)
one decay per second
the time for the activity (or number of unstable nuclei) to halve
cannot be predicted for an individual nucleus

starter: Bismillah. Complete: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ?
State what ionisation means.
Halve 640 four times.

teach.heading: Activity and randomness
bullets: Decay is random: we cannot say when a given nucleus decays
Activity: decays per second, in becquerels (Bq)
The activity falls over time as fewer nuclei remain
Half-life: time for the activity to halve
teach.note: Use a dice simulation: roll 100 dice, remove sixes, repeat. The numbers fall approximately exponentially. Stress random for each nucleus, but predictable for a large number. Half-life values range from fractions of a second to billions of years.

teach.heading: Half-life calculation
bullets: Number of half-lives = time ÷ half-life
Halve the activity that many times
Activity never reaches exactly zero
teach.note: Do the steps visibly. Typical pitfall: halving the time instead of the activity. Another: taking two half-lives as 'all gone'.

model.problem: A source has an activity of 800 Bq. Its half-life is 6.0 hours. Find its activity after 24 hours.

teach.heading: Finding half-life from data
bullets: Read the time for the activity to fall to half
Subtract background first
Check with a second half to be sure
teach.note: Use a graph with a decay curve. Show the method: draw lines from 640 to 320 and from 320 to 160; the time between each halving is the same. The count rates need background correction.

model.problem: The activity of a sample is 640 Bq at 0 min and 320 Bq at 15 min. Find its half-life and its activity at 45 min.
steps: Activity halves in 15 min, so half-life = 15 min
model.answer: Half-life = 15 min; activity at 45 min = 80 Bq

teach.heading: Check: half-life
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Option C confuses half-life with total decay time. Option D halves the half-life. Ask for justification.

check.q: A sample has a half-life of 10 days. What fraction of the unstable nuclei remain after 30 days?
check.why: 30 days is 3 half-lives, so (1/2)³ = 1/8 remain. It does not reach zero.

practice: A source has an initial activity of 1200 Bq and a half-life of 2.0 minutes. Find its activity after 8.0 minutes.
A sample's count rate falls from 480 per minute to 60 per minute in 18 hours. Find its half-life.
Explain why a source with a half-life of 5 seconds is no use for checking pipes underground.
independent: Core: Define half-life in your own words.
Extend: A measured count rate of 84/min includes a background of 4/min. After 20 minutes the measured count is 24/min. Find the half-life.
Stretch: A nuclear waste has half-life 30 years and activity 4000 Bq. How many years until it falls below 100 Bq? Give your answer to the nearest 10 years.
exit: State the unit of activity.
Calculate activity after 3 half-lives if it starts at 960 Bq.
lessons.homework: Draw a decay graph for a sample of 1000 Bq with a half-life of 10 minutes for 0 to 50 minutes, labelling each half-life on the graph.
lessons.send: SEND: give a halving table to complete. EAL: pre-teach decay, halve, background. Stretch: link random decay to the exponential equation.

lessons.title: Uses and dangers of radiation: irradiation and contamination
lessons.bigQuestion: How can the same kind of radiation save a life in hospital and also be dangerous?
objectives: Describe uses of radiation in smoke detectors, thickness monitoring, tracers, sterilisation and cancer treatment
Distinguish contamination from irradiation
Describe the dangers of ionising radiation and precautions
successCriteria: All: give two uses of radiation
Most: justify the type and half-life of a source for a given use
Some: compare contamination and irradiation risks for alpha, beta and gamma
lessons.crossCurricular: Medicine: imaging and radiotherapy; Food technology: sterilising
lessons.smsc: Moral: weighing benefit and harm; protecting patients and workers

keywords.def: exposure to radiation from a source outside the body; the object does not become radioactive
unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on or in an object or body
a radioactive isotope followed through a system to detect leaks or flow
treating cancer using radiation to kill tumour cells

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the activity of 480 Bq after 3 half-lives.
Name the three types of radiation.
State what ionisation does to cells.

teach.heading: Uses of radiation
bullets: Smoke detector: americium-241 emits alpha particles
Thickness monitoring: beta passes through paper or foil
Tracers: gamma emitters followed in the body or pipes
Sterilising: gamma kills bacteria on food and equipment
Radiotherapy: focused gamma beams destroy cancer cells
teach.note: Ask: why do we choose each type? Smoke detector: alpha ionises air, giving a small current that drops when smoke absorbs alpha. Medical tracers need short half-life so the patient has less exposure.

head: Use
Radiation and half-life
Reason
rows: ionises air; absorbed by smoke; safe in a sealed case
passes through paper, partly absorbed; count changes with thickness
penetrates and kills bacteria; the food does not become radioactive

teach.heading: Choosing the source
bullets: Match the radiation penetration to the task
Short half-life for the body; long half-life for monitoring
Sealed sources reduce contamination risk
teach.note: Use the model as a template for exam answers. A detail: for monitoring thickness, alpha would be completely stopped and gamma would hardly change, so beta is best.

model.problem: Explain why beta radiation is used to monitor the thickness of aluminium foil, but alpha and gamma are not.
steps: Alpha is stopped by even thin foil, so no change would be detected
Gamma passes through almost all of it, so thickness changes hardly alter the count
Beta is partly absorbed, so its count changes with thickness
Long half-life means the source needs little replacement
model.answer: Beta is the only radiation whose count changes noticeably with the foil thickness

teach.heading: Irradiation, contamination and safety
bullets: Irradiation: outside exposure; stops when the source is removed
Contamination: radioactive material on or in you; keeps irradiating
Alpha is most dangerous inside the body
Protection: tongs, lead shielding, distance, short time, sealed storage
teach.note: Radiation workers wear film badges and use gloves, tongs, shielding and distance. Stress that radiation dose affects health through damage to DNA, causing cancer, and high doses cause radiation sickness. Discuss benefits versus risks in medicine, which are carefully controlled.

misconception.wrong: A food that has been irradiated with gamma rays becomes radioactive.
misconception.right: Irradiated food is exposed to radiation but nothing radioactive is transferred, so it is not radioactive. Contamination would require radioactive atoms to get on or in the food.

teach.heading: Check: contamination
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Option A is the common mix-up. Option D confuses 'dangerous outside' and 'dangerous inside'.

options: Radiation passes through a patient from an X-ray tube
Radioactive atoms get on the skin or are swallowed
A source is kept in a lead box
check.why: Contamination means radioactive material is on or in the body. Option A describes irradiation.

practice: Explain why a smoke detector contains an alpha source.
Give two precautions for someone handling a radioactive source.
Explain why a tracer injected into a patient should have a short half-life.
independent: Core: State the difference between irradiation and contamination.
Extend: A hospital uses a gamma source for sterilising instruments. Explain why gamma is used and why the instruments are not radioactive afterwards.
Stretch: Evaluate the use of radiotherapy for cancer, considering benefits, risks and how risks are reduced.
exit: Give one use of gamma radiation.
State why alpha is most dangerous when inside the body.
lessons.homework: Write a fact file on one use of radioactivity, covering radiation type, half-life, why it is suitable and safety precautions.
lessons.send: SEND: give a table with use / radiation / reason to match. EAL: pre-teach irradiate, contaminate, tracer. Stretch: explain the ALARA principle.

lessons.title: Nuclear fission and fusion
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a tiny amount of uranium release so much energy, and why is fusion so hard to achieve on Earth?
objectives: Describe nuclear fission and the chain reaction
Describe the parts of a fission reactor and their functions
Describe nuclear fusion and the conditions needed
successCriteria: All: state what fission and fusion are
Most: explain a chain reaction and the roles of the control rods and moderator
Some: compare fission and fusion and explain the conditions for fusion
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: energy changes; Geography: energy supply
lessons.smsc: Moral: weighing great benefit and great risk with responsibility

keywords.def: a large nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons
neutrons from fission cause further fissions
two small nuclei join to form a larger nucleus, releasing energy
material that slows neutrons so they can cause fission

starter: Bismillah. State the number of protons and neutrons in ²³⁵₉₂U.
State what alpha decay is.
State one advantage of nuclear power.

teach.heading: Fission and the chain reaction
bullets: A slow neutron hits a uranium-235 nucleus
The nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei and 2 or 3 neutrons
Energy is released as kinetic energy of the fragments
The new neutrons go on to cause more fissions: a chain reaction
teach.note: Draw the chain reaction as a tree of arrows. Unchecked, it is explosive: a nuclear weapon. In a reactor the rate is controlled. The energy comes from conversion of nuclear potential energy to kinetic energy and then thermal energy.

model.problem: Check this fission equation is balanced: ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3 ¹₀n.
model.answer: The equation is balanced for mass number and atomic number

teach.heading: Inside a nuclear reactor
bullets: Fuel rods: uranium-235 undergoes fission
Control rods (boron): absorb neutrons to control the rate
Moderator (water or graphite): slows neutrons
Coolant: carries thermal energy to make steam for the turbines
Thick concrete shielding absorbs radiation
teach.note: Draw the reactor core. Ask: what happens if the control rods are lowered? (More neutrons absorbed: slower reaction.) The moderator slows the neutrons because fast neutrons are less likely to cause fission. Emphasise the reactor produces heat, the rest is the same as a normal power station.

head: Part
Function
rows: absorb neutrons: raised or lowered to control the rate
slows neutrons so fission is more likely
removes the heat to make steam

teach.heading: Nuclear fusion
bullets: Two light nuclei join to make a heavier nucleus
Energy is released
Needs very high temperature and pressure to overcome repulsion of positive nuclei
Occurs in stars, including the Sun
teach.note: Link to Physics 8 stellar evolution. Fusion happens in the cores of stars because the temperature and pressure are huge (millions of degrees). On Earth, containing the very hot plasma is a challenge, which is why fusion power stations are still experimental.

right.title: Fusion
points: Needs very high temperature and pressure
Little long-lived waste but hard to achieve

teach.heading: Check: control rods
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Option C is a typical error: control rods do not slow neutrons; that is the moderator's job.

check.q: What is the job of the control rods in a nuclear reactor?
options: to absorb neutrons and control the reaction rate
check.why: Control rods absorb neutrons. Lowering them in decreases the rate of fission. The moderator slows neutrons; the coolant carries heat away.

practice: Explain what is meant by a chain reaction.
State two differences between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.
Explain why a nuclear reactor has thick concrete walls.
independent: Core: Describe the function of the moderator and control rods.
Extend: Complete and balance: ²H + ³H → ⁴He + ¹n by checking mass numbers and atomic numbers (Z = 1 for each hydrogen isotope).
Stretch: Evaluate nuclear fission as the main source of electricity for a country, giving two advantages and two disadvantages and a conclusion.
exit: State what fusion is.
State why fusion needs very high temperature.
lessons.homework: Draw and label a diagram of a nuclear reactor and write a sentence for the function of each part.
lessons.send: SEND: give a labelled reactor diagram and a function matching task. EAL: pre-teach split, join, moderator, absorb. Stretch: explain mass defect qualitatively.

lessons.title: Orbits: planets, moons, satellites and comets
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a comet speed up as it swings in towards the Sun, and why can a satellite stay above one place on Earth?
objectives: Explain how gravity keeps bodies in orbit
Compare circular and elliptical orbits for planets and comets
Describe types of satellite orbit and use v = 2πr ÷ T
successCriteria: All: state that gravity provides the force for orbits
Most: describe how speed and period vary with orbit radius and describe different satellite orbits
Some: calculate orbital speed and explain comet motion
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: satellites in weather and mapping; Maths: circumference
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the order and regularity of heavenly bodies, studied by Muslim astronomers such as Ibn al-Haytham, al-Battani and al-Biruni

keywords.def: the curved path of one body around another due to gravity
an object that orbits a larger body, natural (Moon) or artificial
an icy body in a very elliptical orbit around the Sun
orbit above the equator with period 24 hours, so the satellite stays above one point

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the circumference of a circle of radius 5.0 m.
State what gravity does between two masses.
State the speed equation.

teach.heading: Gravity and orbits
bullets: Gravity provides the force that keeps a body in orbit
The body is always changing direction: its velocity is changing
Closer orbits: faster speed and shorter period
Planets: nearly circular orbits around the Sun
teach.note: The existing lessons already introduce gravity and the Solar System; this lesson extends to varied orbits. Use a ball on a string to show the need for a force towards the centre. Ask: what would happen if gravity switched off? (The body moves off in a straight line.)
cycle: Gravity pulls the satellite towards the planet
The satellite moves sideways at high speed
The path curves round the planet
The speed and radius must match to keep a stable orbit

teach.heading: Orbital speed
bullets: Speed = distance ÷ time
Orbital speed v = 2πr ÷ T
r from the centre of the body being orbited
T = time for one orbit in seconds
teach.note: Convert days or years into seconds with care. Link to the circumference 2πr. The result is average speed along the orbit.

model.problem: The Earth orbits the Sun at an average radius of 1.5 × 10¹¹ m in one year (3.15 × 10⁷ s). Calculate its orbital speed.

teach.heading: Comets and elliptical orbits
bullets: Comets have very elliptical orbits
Fastest close to the Sun, slowest when far away
Gravity is stronger when near, so the comet speeds up
The tail forms as the Sun heats the ice and gas
teach.note: Draw the ellipse with the Sun at one focus. Halley's comet has a period of about 76 years. Ask: where has the comet the greatest kinetic energy? (Closest to the Sun.) Planets also have elliptical orbits, but they are almost circular.

misconception.wrong: A comet's tail trails behind it as it moves.
misconception.right: The tail always points away from the Sun, because it is blown away by the Sun's radiation and the solar wind, even when the comet moves towards the Sun.

teach.heading: Artificial satellites
bullets: Low polar orbit: period about 90 min, passes over poles; monitoring and mapping
Geostationary: 24 h period, above the equator; TV and communications
Geostationary orbits are far higher than low orbits
Higher orbit: slower speed and longer period
teach.note: Use the model to calculate the speed of a geostationary satellite. Remind pupils that all geostationary satellites orbit above the equator at the same height.

model.problem: A geostationary satellite orbits at a radius of 4.2 × 10⁷ m from the Earth's centre with a period of 24 hours (86 400 s). Calculate its orbital speed.

teach.heading: Check: orbit change
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Option A is the common idea that satellites are beyond gravity. Option C reverses the relationship.

check.q: Compared with a satellite in a low orbit, a satellite in a higher orbit has...
check.why: Higher orbits have weaker gravity, so the satellite moves more slowly and takes longer for one orbit.

practice: Calculate the orbital speed of the Moon, at 3.8 × 10⁸ m radius, with period 2.4 × 10⁶ s.
Explain why a geostationary satellite is useful for TV broadcasting.
Describe how the speed of a comet changes in its orbit and explain why.
independent: Core: Describe the difference between a low polar orbit and a geostationary orbit.
Extend: The ISS orbits at 6.8 × 10⁶ m from Earth's centre in 92 minutes. Calculate its speed in m/s.
Stretch: Explain why a satellite can't be geostationary above London.
exit: State the source of the force that keeps a planet in orbit.
State where a comet moves fastest.
lessons.homework: Draw an elliptical orbit for a comet with the Sun marked and annotate the speed at three positions.
lessons.send: SEND: give an orbit diagram to annotate with arrows. EAL: pre-teach elliptical, geostationary, period. Stretch: derive the orbital speed from gravitational force (beyond the specification).

lessons.title: From stars to the Big Bang: explaining the universe in exam terms
lessons.bigQuestion: What evidence do scientists use to describe how stars form and how the universe developed?
objectives: Describe the scale of the universe and the order of stellar life cycles
Use an HR diagram and absolute magnitude to compare stars
Explain how red-shift and the cosmic microwave background are used as evidence for the Big Bang model
successCriteria: All: order the stages in the life cycle of a star
Most: explain how the evidence supports the Big Bang model
Some: write a developed six-mark explanation using evidence and reasoning
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: standard form and ratios; History of science: how models change with evidence
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflection on the vastness of the universe and the care taken in testing ideas against evidence

keywords.def: the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m
a measure of the true brightness of a star, as it would appear from a standard distance
the stretching of light from distant galaxies towards longer wavelengths
microwave radiation arriving from all directions, the remnant of the early universe

starter: Bismillah. Name the two main fusion fuels in stars (hydrogen and helium).
State the order of colours of stars from hottest to coolest.
State the equation speed = distance ÷ time.

teach.heading: Scale of the universe
bullets: Solar System: the Sun and objects orbiting it
Galaxy: billions of stars held together by gravity
The Milky Way is about 100 000 light-years across
The universe contains billions of galaxies
teach.note: This consolidates Physics 8 content that earlier lessons cover. Do the light-year calculation: the light-year is a distance, not a time. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

model.problem: Calculate the distance in metres of one light-year. (Speed of light 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s; 1 year = 3.15 × 10⁷ s.)

teach.heading: Life cycles of stars
bullets: Nebula collapses under gravity to form a protostar
Main sequence: hydrogen fuses to helium for most of the star's life
Sun-like star: red giant, then white dwarf
Massive star: red supergiant, supernova, then neutron star or black hole
teach.note: Pupils should be able to state each sequence in order, give the cause of each change (fuel running out and balance of forces changing), and explain that heavier elements are made in stars and scattered by supernovae. Link to the HR diagram.

teach.heading: Reading the HR diagram
bullets: x-axis: surface temperature, hotter to the left
y-axis: absolute magnitude or luminosity; brighter to the top
Main sequence: a diagonal band
Red giants: top right; white dwarfs: bottom left
teach.note: Say that lower (more negative) absolute magnitude means brighter. Ask: a star is cool but very bright; where is it and what size? (Top right: red giant, very large.) Compare absolute magnitude (true brightness) with apparent brightness, which depends on distance.

teach.heading: Big Bang: the evidence
bullets: Model: universe began small, hot, dense about 13.8 billion years ago, and expands
Red-shift: light from distant galaxies is shifted to longer wavelengths
More distant galaxies show greater red-shift, so move away faster
CMB: microwave radiation from all directions, the cooled remnant of the early universe
teach.note: Teach this as the model the specification requires pupils to know and use, with its evidence. Do not editorialise. Evidence: red-shift tells us space is expanding; the CMB was predicted by the model and observed, which supports it. Ask: what would different observations have meant for the model?

model.problem: Explain how red-shift provides evidence for the Big Bang model.
steps: Light from distant galaxies has longer wavelengths than expected
Longer wavelength means the galaxies are moving away from us
Farther galaxies show greater red-shift, so they move away faster
Everything moving apart suggests the universe is expanding from a common starting point
model.answer: Red-shift shows the universe is expanding, which supports the Big Bang model

teach.heading: Check: the CMB
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Option C confuses red-shift and CMB. Option A is a typical statement but not a reason. Ask for the link between evidence and model.

check.q: Why does the cosmic microwave background support the Big Bang model?
options: It shows galaxies are moving apart
It is radiation from the hot early universe, stretched by expansion into microwaves
It proves the universe is infinite
check.why: The Big Bang model predicts radiation left over from the hot early universe, observed today as microwaves from all directions.

practice: Calculate the distance to a star 8.0 light-years away in metres.
State the order of the stages of a massive star's life cycle.
Describe how red-shift evidence shows the universe is expanding.
independent: Core: Complete a table of star types with temperature, brightness and HR position.
Extend: Explain why a red giant is brighter than the Sun even though its surface is cooler.

Stretch: Write a six-mark answer: 'Explain how the evidence from red-shift and the cosmic microwave background supports the Big Bang model.' Use at least two linked statements for each piece of evidence.
exit: State two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang model.
State what becomes of the Sun at the end of its life.
lessons.homework: Create a revision poster showing the life cycle of a Sun-like star and a massive star, with one sentence on the forces involved at each stage.
lessons.send: SEND: sequencing cards for the life cycle and sentence starters for the six-mark answer. EAL: pre-teach galaxy, red-shift, evidence. Stretch: use the red-shift equation z = Δλ ÷ λ = v ÷ c.
